chef_bio.background: TETSU began in 2005 as a tiny 10-tsubo (about 33 sqm) shop in Sendagi, Tokyo, founded by Kazunori Komiya. chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a rich pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) tsukemen — a triple soup of chicken bones, pork bones and bonito/mackerel — served with extra-thick straight noodles that stand up to the heavy dipping broth. Miso and spicy-miso dipping versions are also popular here, and the kitchen rounds out the menu with a chashu rice bowl and a chuka-soba.

anecdotes.text: TETSU's trademark move solves tsukemen's classic weak point of broth going lukewarm: a stone heated until scorching is dropped into the dipping broth partway through the meal so it stays piping hot until the final drop — though this hot-stone service is not available at the AEON Mall food-court branch.
Founder Kazunori Komiya turned a 3-million-yen, 10-tsubo Sendagi shop opened in 2005 into a roughly 30-location tsukemen chain.

chef_bio.background: Iwasaki Tanmen opened its doors on March 1, 2023 in the Ono neighborhood of Yamashina, just steps from Ono Station, taking over a storefront that previously housed another ramen shop (Shioemon). It is a rarity in Kyoto: a shop devoted to tanmen, a vegetable-piled salt ramen far more common in the Kanto region of eastern Japan than here in Kansai.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make-it-your-own simplicity: diners can dial the vegetables, pork, noodle quantity, garlic and spice to taste, and garlic is served on the side so each guest controls their own portion. Sides like gyoza, karaage and takana rice round out an honest, affordable bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The house tanmen is the signature: a mound of lightly stir-fried vegetables — cabbage, bean sprouts and more — over medium straight noodles in a chicken-and-pork salt (shio) broth. It arrives looking hearty and Jiro-esque, yet the soup is surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy back-fat. A pot of house chili-miso (kara-miso) sits at hand so you can stir in heat and depth gradually as you eat.

anecdotes.text: The shop offers several tanmen styles beyond the original — a shio-tonkotsu, a rich miso and a spicy version — so regulars can rotate through the lineup.
One local blogger called the proprietor very kind and admitted he came back years after his first visit because he simply could not forget the tanmen.
The bowl starts around 690 yen, keeping it genuinely budget-friendly.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms the March 2023 opening in Yamashina-Ono near Ono Station in the former Shioemon space, the Kanto-style tanmen (rare in Kyoto) on a light chicken-pork shio broth, four tanmen varieties (classic/shio-tonkotsu/miso/spicy), customizable veg/pork/garlic-on-the-side/spice, kara-miso, gyoza/karaage/takana-rice sides, ~¥690, and 16 seats.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetables are stir-fried together with pork, and the broth is chicken/pork based, so vegetable toppings share animal ingredients and equipment.

chef_bio.origin: Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto — on the city's famous Ichijoji ramen street, but a deliberate step away from the heavy-broth pack.
chef_bio.background: The shop is the latest evolution of a Kyoto noodle maker who has spent years chasing dashi rather than richness. The lineage runs from a dashi-based ramen shop, Isao (イサオ, opened 2010), which the owner renamed and reframed in 2014 as Odashi to Komugi 130 (おだしと小麦 一三〇) to put the dashi and the wheat front and center. In June 2022 the concept was distilled again into だし料理 十.
chef_bio.philosophy: The whole place is built so customers can actually understand dashi — you can watch it being made, taste it, and talk it through with the owner. Seasoning is pared back to almost nothing so the stock itself carries the bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the breakfast-only o-dashi no new-men: a clear soup built from just three things — Rishiri kombu, sawara (young Spanish mackerel / sagoshi), and bonito flakes — seasoned with a single gram of Iwate salt and no soy sauce at all. The noodles are made in-house from domestic wheat and egg, cut to roughly 1mm square and dusted with Hokkaido corn flour, then finished with hand-shaved bonito and a few pieces of salt-cured pepper.

anecdotes.text: By late afternoon the shop sheds its noodle-counter identity and becomes a dashi retail shop and small sake bar, selling drinkable dashi (nomu o-dashi) and easy dashi kits so people can take the craft home.
Tasters describe being unexpectedly moved by the bowl — 出汁のふくよかな香りとまろやかな口当たり (the rich aroma and rounded mouthfeel of the dashi genuinely move you).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: life-info and Tabelog (former name 'Odashi&Wheat isao') confirm owner Inoue, the lineage Isao (2010) -> おだしと小麦 一三〇 (2014) -> だし料理 十 (June 2022), the breakfast-only o-dashi new-men (Rishiri kombu, sawara, bonito, 1g Iwate salt, no soy; ~1mm domestic wheat-egg noodles with Hokkaido corn flour; hand-shaved bonito and salt-cured pepper), and the afternoon dashi-retail/sake-bar with nomu o-dashi and dashi kits.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The house-made noodles are cut from domestic wheat (and egg) in-house, so flour is handled on-site; a shared-kitchen wheat environment should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature dashi bowl uses no soy sauce at all — it is seasoned with about 1 gram of Iwate salt only — so the usual wheat-shoyu tare risk is absent from the broth (the wheat comes from the noodles instead).

vegan_cross_contact.text: The dashi is animal-based throughout (sawara/Spanish mackerel and bonito alongside kombu), and the noodles contain egg, so there is no clean vegan or vegetarian path.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: 「利尻昆布、さわら、まぐろ節で出汁を引き」 — Rishiri kombu, sawara and まぐろ節 (dried TUNA flakes). Noodles: 「国産小麦と卵のみを使用した…自家製麺」.

positives.text: Because the owner makes and explains the dashi in front of guests, it is easy to ask exactly what is in the bowl, and the seasoning is unusually transparent: kombu, sawara, bonito, salt, and house wheat-and-egg noodles.
positives.source_wording: 「料理や小売り、情報発信を通して「出汁を知ってもらいたい」と昨年6月オープン。店主・井上さんが出汁を引く様子を見て、味わって、話を聞けば自然と出汁が身近に感じられる。」

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run dashi specialist where the proprietor talks you through the craft; some Japanese (or a translation app) goes a long way, and a quiet, curious attitude fits the room.

chef_bio.background: Kyoto Kitayama Motomachi Ramen traces its roots to a street cart (yatai) that the first-generation owner — a native of Kanazawa — set up on Shinmachi-dori in Kyoto's Kitayama district roughly 50 years ago. Drawing on the rich, dark soy-sauce style of nearby Toyama Black, he built a Kyoto take on the bowl using tamari soy sauce from a long-established local soy-sauce maker. The business later moved into a permanent shop, settling at its current location in an alley off Higashinotoin in central Kyoto, where the cart's original flavor is carried on by a later (third) generation.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honor the original yatai flavor while continuing to refine it; serve until the broth is gone and then close for the day.
chef_bio.specialty: A rich black-soy-sauce ramen finished with plenty of back fat (背脂醤油らーめん), with beef-tendon ramen (牛すじらーめん) as a second signature. The defining element is a specialty tamari soy sauce of the kind used for eel sauce, sourced from a 160-year-old Kyoto soy-sauce maker.

anecdotes.text: The founder, from Kanazawa, based his recipe on the dark, bold style of Toyama Black but reinterpreted it for Kyoto using local tamari soy sauce.
The shop began as a Kitayama Shinmachi street cart about 50 years ago, and a later (third) generation continues the cart's original taste at the current shop.
The tamari soy sauce is supplied by a 160-year-old established Kyoto soy-sauce shop (Sawai) and is of the type used for eel sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms the 創業50年 Kitayama Shinmachi yatai origin, a Kanazawa-born first-generation owner inspired by 富山ブラック, the specialty たまり醤油 (eel-sauce type) from a 160-year-old Kyoto maker (Sawai), the 背脂醤油らーめん (¥900) and 牛すじらーめん (¥1,100), the Higashinotoin 京町家 location, and continuation by a third generation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is built on a tamari/black soy sauce tare; tamari and standard soy sauce here are wheat-containing and central to the broth.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth and toppings are pork/beef based (beef tendon is a signature), so no item is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A cash-only, counter-style local ramen shop with no English service signaled; basic Japanese or a translation app will make ordering smoother.

chef_bio.background: Mika Nakatani is a French-trained pastry chef from Nantan City in Kyoto Prefecture. Japanese sources report she trained in France and, back in Japan, worked as a pâtissière — including a stint at the celebrated Kyoto restaurant Gion Sasaki (祇園さゝ木) and at patisseries and hotels in Kyoto and Osaka — before going independent around 2016. She converted the shop in September 2021 into a dedicated vegan and gluten-free patisserie, rebuilding her entire repertoire around organic, plant-based, rice-flour ingredients. Her signature is the '0%チーズケーキ' — a cheesecake with gluten, white sugar and animal ingredients all at 0%, built on soy-milk yogurt and cashews.
chef_bio.philosophy: Aims to create 'cute and delicious vegan sweets that nourish the heart' (心が満たされるかわいらしく美味しいヴィーガンスイーツを目指します); shifted to plant-based & gluten-free for health and environmental reasons, using organic ingredients and unrefined (beet) sugar.
chef_bio.specialty: 0%チーズケーキ (0% cheesecake) — gluten/white-sugar/animal all 0%, soy-yogurt & cashew based; plus seasonal rice-flour tarts, shortcakes and Mont Blanc.

anecdotes.text: The 0% cheesecake gets its cheese-like richness and refreshing tang from soy-milk yogurt and lemon juice rather than dairy (しっとり上品な口あたり。チーズのコクに豆乳ヨーグルトやレモン果汁が、さわやかな酸味をプラス).
Beyond the Nijo pop-up days, she supplies her plant-based/GF sweets to mumokuteki cafe and to 素食カフェRen (Cafe Ren), which sells the 0% cheesecake by pre-order.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-ethical-market confirms she is a France-trained pâtissière from Nantan who worked at Kyoto/Osaka hotels before going independent ~2016 and relaunched the shop in Sept 2021 as a fully gluten-free, white-sugar-free, plant-based rice-flour patisserie with the flagship 0% cheesecake; japanese-heart independently confirms a prior pâtissière role at 祇園ささ木 (Gion Sasaki) alongside her France training. Specific French patisserie names given by some profiles could not be verified and were dropped.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Patisserie only — no savory soy-sauce dishes. The 0% cheesecake uses white miso (白味噌) and kuzu; miso can be a hidden wheat/barley source, so confirm the miso is GF if highly sensitive.

vegan_cross_contact.text: No animal products are used anywhere in the shop (fully plant-based), so animal cross-contact is not a concern.

kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.gf_detail: A 99-year-old Kyoto rice merchant (廣瀬米穀店, est. 1926) that sells no wheat products, with an attached café whose owner is a certified 米粉マイスター (rice-flour master) and 五ツ星お米マイスター. Because it is a food shop and rice mill rather than a certified dedicated gluten-free kitchen, celiac guests should still confirm on the day that no wheat is handled or stored on-site. In practice the entire product line is rice-based, so cross-contact risk is low.
kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.vegan_detail: The お米パン / こめやパン rice bread is fully plant-based — made only from rice, rice oil, maple, salt, rice starter (米種), yeast and water — so it is suitable for vegans (sold Wednesdays / by pre-order). The signature 米粉シフォンケーキ and its rusk contain egg and are not vegan. Small baked snacks (scones, snowballs) may contain dairy, so ask before ordering.

kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.notes: [GF] A genuinely useful stop for celiacs just south of Kyoto Station: a century-old rice merchant with an attached café where everything is 100% rice flour and the shop sells no wheat products at all. Grab a 米粉シフォンケーキ (rice-flour chiffon, Tue–Sat) or, on Wednesdays, freshly baked お米パン rice bread. Confirm the day's baking schedule (chiffon Tue–Sat, bread Wed) and that lunch/café-gohan service is running, as it has been paused at times. Small neighborhood shop — assume cash.

chef_bio.chef_name: 廣瀬弘香 (Hirose Hiroka) — 米粉マイスター / 五ツ星お米マイスター
roles: 五ツ星お米マイスター Prof (five-star rice master, professional grade)
米粉パンマイスター (rice-flour bread master)
chef_bio.origin: Originally from Okayama; studied fine art at a design university, then married into the third-generation Hirose rice-merchant family in Higashi-Kujo, Minami-ku, Kyoto.
chef_bio.background: 廣瀬米穀店 was founded in 昭和元年 (1926) and is now in its third generation, giving it roughly 99 years of history as a Kyoto rice merchant. Around 2014, after the shop stopped wholesaling to a large facility, an empty space opened up in the store; the owner's encounter with rice flour and the question 「米屋にしかできないことってなんだろう？」 (what can only a rice shop do?) led to the 2017 opening of the attached café, お米屋カフェ・ふぇ〜る. 廣瀬弘香 — originally from Okayama and trained in fine art before marrying into the family — holds the 五ツ星お米マイスター qualification (with the professional 'Prof' instructor grade) plus 米粉マイスター and 米粉パンマイスター certifications, and the shop is a 「五ツ星お米マイスター認定店」. The rice used is milled in-house (自家精米) from selected varieties, and all café products are made with 100% rice flour and no wheat flour or white sugar.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner wants to spread rice bread 「グルテンフリーのパンとしてではなく、生米から作る一つのおいしい食べ物として」 — not merely as gluten-free bread, but as a delicious food in its own right made from raw rice. She distinguishes 米粉パン (from rice grown for milling into flour) from her お米パン made from top-grade (一等上質米) whole rice, emphasizing the aroma and natural taste of freshly milled rice.
chef_bio.specialty: 米屋の米粉シフォンケーキ, お米パン（こめやパン）, 米粉ラスク

anecdotes.text: 2014年ごろ大型施設への卸販売を中止して店内に空きスペースが生じ、米粉との出会いから『米屋にしかできないことってなんだろう？』という問いが2017年の『お米屋カフェ・ふぇ〜る』開業につながった。
2023年に京都女性起業家賞・優秀賞、京都商工会議所主催の知恵-1グランプリ チャレンジ部門グランプリを受賞。

kyo_mushiyashinai.gf_detail: [Held at "ask" 2026-08-20] The description below was not traceable to any source, so the GF label is held down until it is. [Adversarial GF review 2026-08-19: dedicated→options. Identity checks out and there is NO same-romaji soba confusion here: this is the soy-milk patisserie at 京都市左京区一乗寺里ノ西町78 (own site 648471.com, Tabelog 26003357, category ケーキ/カフェ), open and trading, and Japanese searches for a same-name Kyoto soba house turned up nothing. The label itself collapses on the shop's OWN documents: their FAQ states 「当店では同じ工房にて乳、卵を使用した商品を製造しております」 and then explicitly disclaims 「ほんの微量でも発症される方については、お客様各位にてご判断いただけますようお願いいたします」 — a shared workshop plus a trace-amount self-disclaimer, which is the opposite of a celiac-safe dedicated facility. Their own site carries no 全商品グルテンフリー or 完全グルテンフリー banner at all; グルテンフリー is a product CATEGORY sitting beside per-item 卵・乳・小麦不使用 labels, and their GF senbei lists plain 醤油 (脱脂加工大豆) with no wheat-free documentation. I also checked the record's cited corroboration and it does not hold: the co-trip article (701134, published 2025-10-04) never says 全商品グルテンフリー — it says GF and vegan is 「もうひとつのコンセプト」 (one of their concepts) — so the quote on the record is misattributed, and a 2018 first-hand Japanese report notes 「小麦を使ってあるケーキもあるから確認したんだよ」.] The operator states 「2023年10月には完全グルテンフリー化の為、生産工場と店舗をリニューアルオープンしました」 (In October 2023 they reopened both the production factory and the shop after renovating them for complete gluten-free conversion), and describes the venue as 全商品グルテンフリー (every product gluten-free). Allergen scope is unusually deep: a dedicated 「ミラクル＊ヴァンヌフ 29」 line is free of 29 designated allergens (29品目アレルゲン物質除去), building on the wheat/dairy/egg-free (小麦・乳・卵不使用) base of all cakes. Principal caveat for celiacs: the kitchen is soy-centric (豆乳/おから), and the signature 豆乳醤油プリン uses 醤油 — confirm they use a gluten-free tamari, though a fully-GF-converted facility would be expected to.
kyo_mushiyashinai.vegan_detail: The house concept is explicitly 「グルテンフリー＆ヴィーガン」. Because the cakes are built on 米粉 (rice flour) and 豆乳 (soy milk) instead of wheat, dairy and egg, a large share of the sweets — puddings, roll cake, brûlée, okara cookies, the 29-allergen ミラクル cakes — are plant-based. Not everything is guaranteed vegan (seasonal afternoon-tea components and some savory items are unconfirmed), so vegan diners should ask per item.
kyo_mushiyashinai.hours_raw: 11:00-18:00 (eat-in L.O. 17:30). Closed Mondays and Tuesdays (regardless of holidays). Some listings show a 10:30 open; as of 2026 in-store offering leans toward pre-ordered whole cakes and baked-good assortments.
kyo_mushiyashinai.notes: [GF-dedicated] Kyoto's rare fully-gluten-free patisserie: in October 2023 the owner rebuilt the production factory and the Ichijoji shop specifically to eliminate gluten, and now markets every product as gluten-free. Cakes use rice flour and soy milk; a dedicated line removes 29 allergens. Celiac risk from cross-contact is minimal by their own claim, but the kitchen leans heavily on soy — one of the 29 they otherwise track — and the soy-sauce pudding should be confirmed as GF tamari. Reservations/pre-orders drive whole cakes; eat-in seats are not reservable.

chef_bio.chef_name: うのゆきこ (Uno Yukiko) — 豆乳パティシエ / soy-milk patissier
chef_bio.background: Uno Yukiko styles herself as 「世界で唯一の豆乳パティシエ」 (the world's only soy-milk patissier) and opened Mushiyashinai in Ichijoji around 2006. In December 2009 an encounter with a boy who had 23 food allergies (23品目の食物アレルギー) pushed her to develop allergy-friendly cakes made from 米粉 and 豆乳 rather than wheat and dairy, and by 2020 she completed a cake free of 29 allergens (29品目のアレルゲン不使用). In October 2023 she renovated both the production factory and the shop expressly to convert the whole operation to gluten-free. kyo_bakery_house_creek.gf_detail: Creek is a large everyday neighborhood bakery in Saiin that runs a genuine 米粉100％ (100% rice flour) gluten-free line alongside roughly 80 conventional wheat breads. The shop advertises 米粉を100％使用したグルテンフリーのパン and describes its signature 米粉100％グルテンフリー食パン as 卵・乳製品・小麦粉を一切使わず (using absolutely no egg, dairy, or wheat flour). Because the very same premises bakes and slices wheat bread all day, airborne wheat flour and shared equipment mean cross-contact is realistic — this is an OPTIONS venue, not a dedicated celiac-safe one. Celiacs should treat the rice-flour items as allergen-recipe products, not contamination-controlled ones.
kyo_bakery_house_creek.vegan_detail: The flagship 米粉100％グルテンフリー食パン is explicitly 卵・乳製品・小麦粉不使用 (no egg, dairy, or wheat), so it is incidentally vegan, and some rice-flour cookies may follow. Most of the ~80 breads, however, are standard wheat products with butter/dairy, so vegan choices are limited to a handful of the rice-flour line. Confirm ingredients per item, as recipes vary.
kyo_bakery_house_creek.hours_raw: 8:00–22:00, open daily (no regular closing day). Note: some listings cite 7:00–20:30 — confirm before visiting.
kyo_bakery_house_creek.notes: [GF] Ask staff directly for the 米粉100％ (100% rice flour) items — the gluten-free 食パン (loaf), rice-flour bagels, cookies and cheesecake. These are made to an egg/dairy/wheat-free recipe, but everything is produced in a shared, high-volume wheat bakery with visible flour dust, so this suits gluten-sensitive/allergy-aware diners rather than highly reactive celiacs. Buy sealed/whole items rather than open-shelf loose bread to reduce cross-contact, and go early as the GF line sells out.

kyo_nicole_naturelle.gf_detail: THE NICOLE is a conventional Kyoto patisserie that also runs a separate allergen-free sub-line, Nicole Naturelle, whose sweets are made with 100% domestic rice flour and no wheat. The venue's own site states 『卵、乳製品、小麦粉、動物性油脂は使用しておりません』 and describes the line as 『卵、乳、白砂糖不使用』『グルテンフリー』『ヴィーガンスイーツ』 using 国産米粉100%. However, the SAME shop bakes ordinary wheat flour cakes and serves 欧風スパイスカレー (European-style spice curry, typically a wheat-roux base), so the kitchen is shared and cross-contact with wheat flour is a real risk — celiacs must confirm the item is from the Naturelle line and ideally order it pre-made/sealed. Because of the shared wheat kitchen this stays an 'options' venue, not a dedicated GF facility.
kyo_nicole_naturelle.vegan_detail: The Nicole Naturelle line is fully plant-based — 卵・乳・動物性油脂不使用, using 京豆腐 (Kyoto tofu), 豆乳ヨーグルト (soy yogurt), soy-based 'butter', coconut oil and maple syrup in place of dairy and eggs. These items are explicitly marketed as ヴィーガンスイーツ. The parent THE NICOLE shop, though, also sells conventional cakes with egg/dairy and non-vegan curry, so only the Naturelle line is vegan — choose from it specifically.

kyo_nicole_naturelle.notes: [GF] The Nicole Naturelle sub-line uses 国産米粉100% and no wheat, but it is baked in the same kitchen as THE NICOLE's ordinary wheat cakes and wheat-roux spice curry — treat as cross-contact risk, not celiac-safe. Order Naturelle items specifically (they are reservation/online-order only, sold mostly as whole tarts, chocolate and sablé tins) and confirm the item is from the allergen line. Cash only; small counter shop in the Horikawa shopping arcade.

chef_bio.background: Owner-pâtissier 堀口微笑琉 was born in 1979 in Kyoto's Nishijin district and trained at several patisseries between 1999 and 2006 before opening his own shop, 洋菓子屋Sorcier, in Umeda in 2008. The business relocated and evolved over the years — becoming Kitchen&Cake NICOLE in 2015 and rebranding as THE NICOLE at the current 西陣 (Nishijin) location in 2019. In 2022 he added a spice-curry operation (麺屋 微笑琉 / NICOLEカレー, a once-a-week spice-curry-udon venture), and in 2023 he launched the Nicole Naturelle allergen-free, vegan, gluten-free sweets line. The shop's stated aim is 「食材の制限がある方も楽しめるスイーツ」— sweets that people with dietary restrictions can also enjoy.
chef_bio.philosophy: A hybrid patisserie-and-curry café built around inclusivity and low-sugar / low-fat, 'body-friendly' sweets, with the Nicole Naturelle line created so that people with egg, dairy and wheat restrictions can still enjoy cakes.

anecdotes.text: The venture is a 洋菓子×スパイスカレー hybrid — a Western-confectionery shop that also serves a meat-free 'Nicole curry' deriving umami from vegetables, plus rotating daily creative spice curries.
The allergen-free Nicole Naturelle line was launched in 2023, years after the base patisserie, specifically to serve customers with dietary restrictions.

kyo_oubon.gf_detail: OUBON is a conventional Western pâtisserie near Fushimi Inari that sells regular wheat cakes AND a separate allergy-oriented 米粉 (rice-flour) line, so wheat is handled in the same kitchen. chef_bio.origin: Tosa (Kōchi Prefecture); the shop is in Kiyamachi, Nakagyo Ward, Kyoto
chef_bio.background: A Tosa (Kōchi) native who by most accounts has spent roughly fifty years cooking, running a small counter izakaya devoted to the food of his home region. He grills over Tosa binchōtan (the prized white charcoal of Kōchi) and centers the menu on Kōchi's most famous dish, seared bonito — the kind of veteran, single-counter kitchen where the chef works in front of you and the seasons drive what's served.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal yakitori over Tosa binchōtan and Kōchi's signature katsuo (bonito) tataki, plus shamo (game-fowl) hot pot and seasonal Tosa dishes.

anecdotes.text: Regulars single out the bonito tataki as thick, generous and completely free of any fishy odor — the hallmark of well-handled katsuo — and note that each yakitori skewer is grilled with real care over binchōtan.

The shop is described as an izakaya serving 'the finest yakitori in Kyoto' by a chef with about 50 years of experience, originally from Tosa in Kōchi Prefecture, with a charming, old-Kyoto exterior that draws both locals and foreign guests.
It sits on Kiyamachi just south of Sanjo, upstairs on the 2nd floor above an Italian restaurant — an easy-to-miss counter that rewards those who seek it out.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese listings (Tabelog 郷土料理/焼き鳥, Retty, hitosara, navikyo, HotPepper) describe 土佐屋室戸 as a small Kōchi (Tosa) izakaya at 河原町通三条下ル大黒町49, entrance on Kiyamachi, on the 2nd floor above an Italian restaurant, with a ~10-seat counter and one small tatami room (6–8). Open Mon–Sat 17:00–23:00, closed Sunday; phone 075-221-3056; reservations accepted. The taishō, a Tosa native, is credited with ~50 years of experience; signatures are binchōtan yakitori, katsuo (bonito) tataki, and shamo hot pot, with seasonal Kōchi fare.

cultural_comfort.note: A small veteran-run counter on Kiyamachi that does see foreign diners and takes online reservations — but it's a Japanese izakaya led by a ~50-year chef, with little to no English. A reservation, a few words of Japanese, and easy counter manners go a long way.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a yakitori-and-izakaya counter, not a celiac-safe kitchen. Skewers are grilled over a shared charcoal grill alongside tare-basted (wheat soy sauce) items, and any battered/fried dishes share oil, so cross-contamination with wheat is likely across the menu.

Naturally gluten-free choices may exist if confirmed — sashimi, salt (shio) skewers, and salt-style katsuo tataki without ponzu — but they must be ordered explicitly shio/no-sauce and confirmed with the chef.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Yakitori tare, ponzu for the katsuo tataki, and nabe broths are built on Japanese soy sauce, which typically contains wheat. Assume these sauces contain gluten unless the chef confirms a wheat-free alternative; ordering shio (salt) avoids the tare.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A fish- and meat-forward Tosa izakaya (bonito, chicken, game-fowl hot pot) with bonito dashi throughout — even vegetable dishes likely carry animal-derived stock. There is no documented vegan menu; confirm each item with the chef.

positives.text: A tiny, owner-run counter where the chef cooks directly in front of you, so you can ask about ingredients and preparation face-to-face — easiest with some Japanese or a translation app.

kyr_fukuchian_nijojo_mae.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The chain's own allergen chart lists wheat (小麦) in every ramen, set, side and topping on it — including the chashu, seasoned egg and menma — and the noodles are made in-house from wheat flour. The shop says it cooks with ordinary shared utensils and dishes and leaves cross-contamination to the diner's own judgment. The only food item the chart shows without wheat is the sherbet. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_fukuchian_nijojo_mae.vegan_detail: The regular bowls are built on a pork-bone and chicken-frame soup and topped with pork; the allergen chart lists pork and chicken for all of them. The shop does advertise a 'vegetarian ramen' (miso-based broth, house-made noodles), but in its own words it is made with 'almost no' (ほぼ) meat or fish ingredients — so do not assume it is vegan. Ask what the remaining animal ingredients are before ordering.
kyr_fukuchian_nijojo_mae.hours_raw: Daily 11:00–21:00 (last order 20:30). Closed over the New Year.
kyr_fukuchian_nijojo_mae.notes: [Ramen · Fukuchiyama chain] The Kyoto-city branch of ふくちあん, a ramen company from Fukuchiyama in northern Kyoto Prefecture, on the northeast corner of the Horikawa-Oike crossing, across the road from Nijō Castle; it opened in 2022. The house bowl is a pork-bone and Tamba chicken-frame soup simmered for 20+ hours, seasoned with a brewed soy tare aged a year in cedar barrels, over thin house-made noodles, and comes with two kinds of pork, a seasoned egg and green onion. Kara-age is the other draw — the shop advertises a Karaage Grand Prix gold award. You buy a ticket at the machine; an English menu is posted outside and many of the customers are overseas visitors. The shop also advertises a miso-based vegetarian ramen.

roles: ramen company (株式会社新福知庵), Fukuchiyama
chef_bio.origin: Fukuchiyama, northern Kyoto Prefecture — the chain's main shop is by JR Fukuchiyama Station
chef_bio.background: Fukuchian began as a change of trade: in 1996 a Fukuchiyama textile firm turned itself into a ramen business and opened the first ふくちあん. The company has since added branches in Kaibara, Kitaōji (Kyoto), Nijō-jō-mae (2022) and Shiga.
chef_bio.philosophy: The founding-spirit essay on the company site: no textbook, soup after soup poured away, and the temptation to make life easier with ready-made soy tare and stock — refused, because "I don't want to tell a lie" (ウソは嫌なんです).
chef_bio.specialty: Ramen in a pork-bone and Tamba chicken soup with a year-aged brewed soy tare and house-made thin noodles; tender kara-age.

anecdotes.text: Fukuchian started in 1996, when 丸三加工, a Fukuchiyama textile company hit by the industry moving overseas, renamed itself 株式会社福知庵 and became a ramen shop. The Nijō-jō-mae branch opened in 2022.

The soup: Japanese pork leg bones are washed, blanched to remove blood and scum, then simmered in a large pot with Tamba chicken frames, negi and plenty of onion — more than 20 hours in all. It is finished with a brewed soy sauce aged a full year in cedar barrels.
The noodles are made in-house from Nisshin's 特ナンバーワン flour with Inner-Mongolian kansui and 天外天 salt, kneaded, layered, rolled and rested before cutting.
The shop advertises a gold award at the Karaage Grand Prix (からあげグランプリ金賞受賞) for its kara-age.

A June 2026 diner noted the English menu posted outside and the overseas customers inside, ordered the 特濃 (extra-rich) Fukuchian ramen, and praised its slightly sweet pork-bone broth with crunchy bean sprouts and thick chashu.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト(fukuchian.jp)より、株式会社新福知庵(福知山市)。平成8年に繊維業の丸三加工が株式会社福知庵に商号変更しラーメン専門店へ業態変更、ふくちあん本店開店。令和4年 二条城前店開店。二条城前店: 京都市中京区東堀川通御池上る押堀町45-1、TEL 075-212-7620、11:00〜21:00(L.O.20:30)、年中無休(年始を除く)、27席。スープは国産げん骨と丹波産鶏ガラを20時間以上炊く豚骨、元ダレは杉樽で一年熟成の本醸造醤油、自家製麺は日清「特ナンバーワン」。アレルギー表では全ラーメン・サイド・トッピングに小麦。Instagram(2026/10/03)でベジタリアンラーメン(味噌ベース、自家製麺、肉・魚の成分を「ほぼ」使用せず)を告知。

cultural_comfort.note: Order and pay at the ticket machine (electronic money and QR payments accepted, no credit cards). An English menu is posted outside and the shop sees many overseas visitors on their way to or from Nijō Castle; expect a queue on weekends.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The chain's allergen chart lists 小麦 (wheat) for every ramen, set, side dish and topping on it, and the shop states it cooks with ordinary kitchen utensils and ordinarily washed dishes, asking diners to judge cross-contamination risk for themselves.
The noodles are made in-house from wheat flour (Nisshin 特ナンバーワン).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The base tare (元ダレ) is a brewed soy sauce (本醸造醤油), combined with the pork-bone soup for every shoyu-style bowl.
On the allergen chart even the toppings — トロチャーシュー, バラチャーシュー, 味玉 and メンマ — list 小麦, so a "no noodles" order does not get you to a wheat-free bowl.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The soup is pork leg bone and Tamba chicken frames simmered together for 20+ hours.
The vegetarian ramen has a miso-based broth and is made with 'almost no' (ほぼ) meat or fish ingredients, in the shop's own words — not stated to be vegan.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The chain publishes a per-dish allergen chart (Japanese) that counts allergens shared during processing or cooking as "contained", not only those in the recipe.
